Seminar Title:

Development of Multiscale Hierarchical FRP Composites through inter-ply Hybrid, Fiber Decoration and Matrix Modification Approaches and their Environmental Durability Analysis

Seminar Type:

Department:

Abstract:

Though CFRP composites exhibit exceptional combination of strength and modulus with ultralight weight and excellent corrosion resistance, their widespread adoption is often slowed down by high material costs (especially carbon fiber) and sensitivity to environmental conditions such as temperature extremes. Addressing these challenges requires innovative approaches that balance performance, cost, and reliability. A symmetric hybrid laminate configuration, C3G6C3 (comprising three carbon fiber layers, six glass fiber layers, and three carbon fiber layers), was developed and compared against a carbon fiber laminate (C12). At room temperature, the C3G6C3 hybrid demonstrates mechanical properties closely matching those of the all-carbon counterpart with its flexural modulus reaches ~100% of C12&rsquos value, while flexural strength and strain at peak load are retained at 96% and 97%, respectively well within a 5% deviation. However, this parity is not sustained as temperature increases, highlighting a limitation in thermal stability for the hybrid architecture under elevated service conditions. To address this performance gap and further enhance mechanical response, two complementary approaches were explored. First, the epoxy matrix was modified by incorporating 1 wt% of a functional additive, which resulted in a notable 18.767% increase in flexural modulus for the C3G6C3 laminate at room temperature. Second, carbon fibers were surface-functionalized via electrophoretic deposition using carboxylated carbon nanotubes (CNTCOOH) at a concentration of 1 g/L, leading to a 17% enhancement in flexural modulus attributed to superior fiber&ndashmatrix interfacial adhesion.

This study investigates the flexural failure mechanics of pure carbon, carbon-glass hybrid, and carbon nanotube (CNT)-reinforced multiscale epoxy laminates subjected to variable liquid nitrogen cryogenic conditioning ranging from a 10-minute surface shock to a 24-hour volumetric saturation. The experimental results demonstrate that while prolonged cryogenic exposure severely degrades the interlaminar shear strength of unmodified hybrids through massive differential thermal contraction, uniformly dispersed CNTs effectively bridge these deep-seated thermal microcracks to fully recover the macroscopic load-bearing capacity and rigidity of the pure carbon baseline.

This study investigates the flexural degradation mechanics of continuous pure carbon and carbon-glass hybrid multiscale laminates both with and without dispersed carbon nanotube (CNT) reinforcement subjected to aggressive environmental thermal cycling between +85&degC and -50&degC. The experimental findings reveal that while the alternating thermodynamic states of elevated-temperature viscoelastic expansion and sub-zero rigid contraction induce severe interlaminar fatigue at the chemically dissimilar transition zones of unmodified hybrids, the uniform dispersion of CNTs restricts bulk polymer chain mobility and efficiently bridges cyclic microcracks to preserve the structural integrity and macroscopic load-bearing capacity of the composite.
